config.prompt: Which demand is elastic and which is inelastic?

items.label: petrol for the daily commute, this month
one brand of cola among many

config.why: Substitutes are the master determinant: a single cola brand has many, insulin has none.

activities.anchor: Using percentage changes rather than raw units
activities.caption: call the elasticity
activities.name: elCafeEst

config.prompt: A café raises its price by 10% and sales fall by 25%. What is the magnitude of PED?
config.why: |PED| = 25% ÷ 10% = 2.5 — elastic. Revenue falls because the quantity effect dominates the price effect.
config.context: ignore the minus sign; compare magnitudes

activities.anchor: What decides whether buyers walk away
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the determinants
activities.name: elDeterminantsCloze

config.text: The master determinant of elasticity is the availability of %%0%%. Necessities with no close substitutes are %%1%%, while luxuries with many alternatives are %%2%%.
config.hint: Market definition matters: one brand is elastic, the whole category much less so.

activities.caption: pair each change with its revenue effect
activities.name: elRevenueMatch

config.prompt: Pair each change with its effect on total revenue:

pairs.left: raise price when demand is inelastic
raise price when demand is elastic
cut price when demand is elastic

config.why: Revenue is price × quantity: the price effect dominates when demand is inelastic, the quantity effect when it is elastic.

activities.anchor: how willingly producers respond to a price signal
activities.caption: trace inelastic housing supply
activities.name: elHousingBranch

config.root: A city's housing demand grows, but planning rules make new supply almost perfectly inelastic. Trace the result.

start.text: Demand shifts right while supply barely responds. What happens to price and quantity?

choices.label: Price rises sharply; quantity barely moves
choices.feedback: Yes — with inelastic supply, demand growth converts almost entirely into higher prices.

choices.label: Quantity rises sharply; price barely moves
choices.feedback: That is the elastic-supply case; planning restrictions prevent it.

choices.label: Both price and quantity fall
choices.feedback: Demand grew, so neither falls — the question is how the gain splits.

rent.text: With supply inelastic, demand growth converts almost entirely into higher prices — the elasticity story behind high rents in London or San Francisco.

qty.text: That would need elastic supply: new building absorbing the demand. Planning restrictions prevent exactly that.

fall.text: Demand grew, so neither price nor quantity falls; the question is how the gain splits.

config.why: Supply elasticity decides whether demand growth becomes more housing or higher rents; restrictive planning makes it mostly the latter.

activities.anchor: Two further dials complete the family
activities.caption: classify a good by income elasticity
activities.name: elIncomeOrder

config.prompt: Classify a good from its income elasticity — put the steps in order:
items: Measure the percentage change in quantity demanded
Divide by the percentage change in income
A positive YED marks a normal good
A YED above 1 marks a luxury; between 0 and 1, a necessity
A negative YED marks an inferior good
config.why: The sign sorts normal from inferior; the size above one separates luxuries from necessities.

activities.anchor: A tax's legal payer and its economic bearer
activities.caption: who bears the tax?
activities.name: elIncidencePlace

config.prompt: A £1 per-unit tax is imposed on a good with perfectly inelastic demand and elastic supply. How much of the £1 do buyers bear? Place it.
config.why: Buyers cannot walk away, so they bear the full £1 and sellers pass it on entirely. With elastic demand and inelastic supply, the burden flips to sellers.

activities.caption: true or false — the time horizon
activities.name: elHorizonJudge

statements.s: Petrol demand is more elastic over ten years than over one month.
statements.why: Over years, drivers can buy smaller cars, move closer to work or switch to public transport.

statements.s: A fuel tax's effect on consumption is fully visible in the first year.
statements.why: The immediate response is small; the structural response builds as vehicles and homes turn over.

statements.s: Long-run elasticities are the relevant number for structural policy questions.
statements.why: Congestion charges, carbon prices and sugar taxes reshape behaviour over years, not weeks.

activities.anchor: Estimated elasticities come from watching natural experiments
activities.caption: find the teenage-elasticity slip
activities.name: elTeenSpot

config.prompt: Find the line where the cigarette-tax reasoning goes wrong:
lines: A cigarette tax raises the price by 10%.
Teenage smoking falls by 7%, so teenage PED is −0.7.
Teenage demand is therefore less elastic than adult demand at −0.4.
Public-health campaigns prefer the teenage number because deterrence is larger there.
That is why a tobacco tax can both raise revenue and reduce smoking.
config.correction: |−0.7| is larger than |−0.4|, so teenage demand is more elastic, not less.
config.why: More elastic means a bigger behavioural response — which is exactly why the teenage figure is the one public-health campaigns buy.

activities.caption: one behaviour, two horizons — drag the divider
activities.name: elHorizonCompare

config.prompt: One behaviour, two horizons — drag the divider:

before.label: short run
before.text: the commute, the car and the appliances are fixed; petrol demand is barely responsive (≈ −0.25)

after.label: long run
after.text: smaller cars, moves closer to work and better insulation; demand stretches (≈ −0.6 or more)

config.why: Elasticities are behaviour under constraints, and constraints loosen with time — which is why the policy answer depends on the horizon you ask about.
